html:
The caste system is India's old order of hereditary social groups, in which people are born into a group that shapes whom they marry, what work they do and how others treat them. It has two layers.

  • Varna is the scheme of four orders set out in Vedic and later texts: Brahmins (priests and scholars), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (traders and farmers) and Shudras (labourers and servants). A hymn of the Rigveda has them born from the body of a cosmic man.
  • Jati is the lived reality: thousands of local birth groups, often tied to a trade, who marry within the group and rank themselves against each other.

Below and outside the four varnas were groups treated as "untouchable", now called Dalits, kept from temples, wells and schools.

The Buddha and bhakti poets such as Kabir taught that birth does not decide worth. British rule hardened caste: the census from 1871 sorted and ranked every group. In the 1800s and 1900s reformers fought back:

  • Savitribai Phule and her husband opened schools for girls and low castes.
  • Periyar's Self-Respect Movement attacked Brahmin dominance in the Tamil south.
  • B. R. Ambedkar, born a Dalit, chaired the drafting of India's constitution, which outlawed untouchability in 1950, and led the mass conversion to Buddhism of 1956.

Seats in schools, jobs and parliament are reserved for the lowest castes, extended to other backward classes by the Mandal Commission quotas in 1990. Caste still shapes marriage and politics in India.
sum: The caste system is India's old order of hereditary social groups, in which people are born into a group that shapes whom they marry, what work they do and how others treat them. It has two layers.
